title: Mississippi Officer Who Shot 1‑Year‑Old Resigns, Says Senatobia Mayor; Community Demands Justice
body:
The Senatoga Police Department confirmed Friday that Sergeant Hunter Foster, the officer who discharged his weapon into a moving vehicle and killed a one‑year‑old boy during a shop‑lifting response, has formally resigned from the force. Mayor Greg Graves announced the departure, saying the decision was made “in the best interest of the department and the community” after weeks of intense scrutiny, legal investigations and public outcry.

The tragic incident occurred on March 23, when officers responded to a report of shoplifting at a local convenience store. As Foster and a partner attempted to stop the suspect’s car, Foster fired several rounds into the vehicle’s rear, striking the infant who was seated in a car seat in the back. The child died at the scene, and the suspect, who survived, was later charged with unlawful possession of a firearm. The shooting ignited a firestorm of criticism over police use‑of‑force policies, especially given that the officer’s target was a moving vehicle and the presence of an innocent child was not known at the time.

State investigators, alongside the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, have concluded that Foster’s actions violated departmental protocol, which requires officers to assess the threat level and prioritize de‑escalation before using lethal force. The report indicated that Foster “failed to consider alternative tactics” and that his decision to fire was “unreasonable under the circumstances.” While the officer was placed on administrative leave pending the investigation, the resignation marks the first concrete personnel action taken by the department in this case.

Community reaction has been a mix of relief and lingering anger. Local residents gathered outside the police station on Tuesday, holding signs that read “Justice for Baby Jalen” and chanting for broader reforms. Civil‑rights groups have called for a comprehensive review of the department’s training and policies, urging state legislators to enact stricter oversight of police shootings. “Resignation does not erase the loss of a child,” said Mariah Thompson, director of the Mississippi chapter of the NAACP. “It is a step, but we need systemic change to prevent another tragedy like this.”

Legal experts note that the resignation does not shield Foster from potential criminal liability. Mississippi law permits the filing of charges against officers whose use of force is deemed unlawful, and the district attorney’s office has indicated that it will consider whether to pursue manslaughter or other charges based on the investigative findings. The city’s legal counsel, meanwhile, is reviewing the department’s liability exposure, as the family of the child has already filed a wrongful‑death lawsuit seeking compensatory damages.

The episode has prompted state officials to reexamine broader policing standards. Governor Tate Reeves announced the formation of a task force to evaluate use‑of‑force guidelines across Mississippi, citing the need for “clear, consistent, and accountable practices.” Lawmakers are expected to introduce legislation that would require mandatory body‑camera footage for all firearm discharges and establish an independent review board to assess officer conduct in shooting incidents.

As Senatoga attempts to heal, the resignation of Sergeant Foster serves as both a symbolic and practical turning point. The department has pledged to overhaul its training curriculum, increase community‑policing initiatives, and engage with external auditors to rebuild trust. Whether these measures will satisfy a grieving community and prevent future tragedies remains to be seen, but the case underscores a growing national demand for transparency and accountability in law‑enforcement actions.
